growth_stages.name: Nursery
growth_stages.description: Seeds sown in nursery bags, typically December to February, then grown for 3 to 7 months before transplanting. Day 0 is transplanting, not seed sowing.

growth_stages.name: Establishment (immature)
growth_stages.description: Young tree growth under shade, not yet bearing. Multiple sources place first bearing at 3 to 5 years after transplanting.

growth_stages.name: Early bearing
growth_stages.description: Pod bearing has begun but yield is still climbing toward the tree's mature potential.

growth_stages.name: Full bearing (recurring)
growth_stages.description: Full productivity, reached 8 to 10 years after transplanting per general guidance. Annual flowering and harvest cycle repeats for roughly 25 to 30 years.

operations.name: Land Clearing
operations.description: Clearing of plot, retaining or planting shade trees.

operations.name: Transplanting
operations.description: Moving seedlings from nursery to field. This is day 0 of the field lifecycle.

operations.name: Shade Management
operations.description: Thinning/adjusting shade cover as tree matures.

operations.name: Pest & Disease Control
operations.description: Black pod, capsid, and other control measures.

operations.name: Harvest (Pod Break)
operations.description: Ripe pod harvesting. Recurs every bearing season once mature.

operations.name: Fermentation
operations.description: Bean fermentation in heaps/boxes, typically 5-7 days.

operations.name: Drying
operations.description: Sun-drying beans to safe moisture content.

validation_rules.condition: Nursery is normally started around the time land clearing and shade preparation begins. Large gaps are flagged but not blocked since the nursery can run on a different plot while the main field is still being prepared.
validation_rules.source: Interval itself is still not tied to a specific named source. Flagged for further confirmation, same as before.

validation_rules.condition: Hard block if the nursery period is under 90 or over 180 days. See cocoa_r2b for the flag.
validation_rules.source: AgTrail Master Agronomist & Validator Ruleset, Agrolinking Solutions Ltd., July 2026, section 15 (Cocoa)

validation_rules.condition: An initial application of organic manure is applied directly into the planting hole at the time of transplanting itself, not weeks later. This is a real change from the previous draft, which assumed a 30 day wait. Later applications then follow roughly every six months as the tree grows. Applies only when the planting is recorded: an orchard established before it was entered here is not blocked for lacking it.
validation_rules.source: How to Plant Cocoa in Nigeria (Floratalk): organic manure applied during transplanting, with additional fertilizer roughly every six months afterward

validation_rules.condition: Hard block if the first harvest is logged before 540 days (1.5 years) after transplanting. Applies only when the planting is recorded: an orchard established before it was entered here is not blocked for lacking it.
validation_rules.source: AgTrail Master Agronomist & Validator Ruleset, Agrolinking Solutions Ltd., July 2026, section 15 (Cocoa)

validation_rules.condition: Hybrids bear from about 2 years. Flagged if the first harvest is logged before 730 days after transplanting. Applies only when the planting is recorded: an orchard established before it was entered here is not blocked for lacking it.
validation_rules.source: AgTrail Master Agronomist & Validator Ruleset, Agrolinking Solutions Ltd., July 2026, section 15 (Cocoa)

validation_rules.condition: Fermentation should begin within a day or two of pod break to avoid quality loss.
validation_rules.source: General cacao post harvest guidance, consistent across sources reviewed, though not tied to one specific named study

validation_rules.condition: Fermentation is expected to last 5-7 days. Flagged if drying is logged under 4 or over 8 days after fermentation was logged. See cocoa_r6_block for the hard block.
validation_rules.source: AgTrail Master Agronomist & Validator Ruleset, Agrolinking Solutions Ltd., July 2026, section 15 (Cocoa)

weather_preferences.notes: Requires shade in early years; sensitive to prolonged dry season without irrigation.

diseases.name: Black Pod Disease
diseases.symptoms: Brown to black lesions spreading over the pod surface, rotting beans inside.
diseases.management: Resistant or tolerant varieties are the most sustainable control. Chemical control works but is expensive relative to typical production value and requires real skill to apply correctly. Sanitation (removing infected pods) and pruning to improve airflow also help.
diseases.source: Cocoa Research Institute of Nigeria research literature: caused mainly by Phytophthora megakarya (over 80 percent of cases in Nigeria) and Phytophthora palmivora (under 20 percent). P. megakarya is the more aggressive of the two. Yield losses run around 30 percent from P. palmivora and up to 80 to 90 percent in poorly maintained farms affected by P. megakarya, with 90 to 100 percent losses recorded in wetter regions.

diseases.name: Cocoa Swollen Shoot Virus (CSSV)
diseases.symptoms: Swelling of shoots and roots, red vein banding on leaves, dieback.
diseases.management: There is no cure once a tree is infected. The only effective response is to identify and remove infected trees and replant with disease free material. Controlling the mealybug vector helps slow spread but does not treat existing infection.
diseases.source: Multiple sources confirm eradication as the only effective treatment for CSSV, including a Ghana focused field study and a Nigeria specific incidence survey. CSSV was first identified in Nigeria in 1944 near Ibadan and is spread tree to tree by several mealybug species.

pests.name: Mirids / Capsids
pests.symptoms: Sucking insects that cause dark, sunken sap lesions on young shoots and pods, which often become infected with disease afterward. Young, unshaded trees are especially vulnerable.
pests.management: Insecticide spraying remains the main control method and is still widely used despite decades of research effort. Maintaining adequate shade in the early years reduces vulnerability.
pests.source: A Southwest Nigeria field survey recorded cocoa mirid presence in 11.44 percent of trees sampled. The two species most implicated across West Africa are Distantiella theobroma and Sahlbergella singularis.

pests.name: Mealybugs
pests.symptoms: Direct feeding damage is minor. Primary importance is as the insect vector that spreads Cocoa Swollen Shoot Virus between trees.
pests.management: Vector control matters more than direct mealybug control. Removing infected neighboring trees reduces the reservoir of virus available for mealybugs to spread.
pests.source: Planococcoides njalensis and Planococcus citri are identified as the most significant vector species in the Nigeria specific CSSV literature reviewed.

pests.name: Termites
pests.symptoms: Not detailed in the sources reviewed beyond general presence.
pests.management: Not detailed in the sources reviewed. Flagged as an area needing further research before any farmer facing guidance is written for it.
pests.source: The same Southwest Nigeria field survey that recorded mirid incidence recorded termites at 13.16 percent of trees sampled, higher than mirids, but the source did not go into management detail.

yield_model.notes: These figures were not independently re-sourced during this revision. They remain from the original draft and confidence has been lowered slightly rather than raised, since the sourcing pass this time focused on timing rules and pest and disease data, not yield numbers specifically. Treat this as still needing its own dedicated sourcing pass. Updated 2026-10-25: the earlier expected figure was 0.3 - 0.8 (immature/early bearing), 0.6 - 1.2 (full bearing) (tonnes dry beans), from older sources. FAO's national average for 2024 is 0.27 t/ha, so that figure was replaced; see harvest_estimate for the sources.

version_history.summary: Initial structured template for a perennial tree crop, built to stress-test the schema against annual-crop assumptions (repeating harvest, non-standard day-zero via nursery). NOT yet validated by an agronomist.
version_history.source: Draft / general references (IITA, CRIN public guidance) - pending expert review

version_history.changed_by: AgTrail Knowledge Base - sourced revision pass
version_history.summary: Replaced every previously unsourced timing rule, disease entry, and pest entry with numbers checked against named sources, matching the standard already applied to Maize and Cassava. Key changes: fertilizer now correctly applied at transplanting via organic manure rather than 30 days later; nursery duration widened to 90 to 210 days to honestly reflect a real conflict between two sources rather than picking one; harvest timing split into a conservative 2 year hard block plus a 3 to 5 year typical warning window, with an explicit flag on a single promotional source claiming 18 month hybrid bearing that is not corroborated anywhere else; black pod disease and swollen shoot virus rewritten with actual species names, transmission mechanisms, and cited yield loss figures instead of generic descriptions; added termites as a pest, though its entry is itself flagged as needing further detail. One notable finding not yet built into the file: CRIN's own literature states fertilizer requirements have been established separately for different soil zones, the southwest ecological zone, the sandy soils of Edo State, and the heavy rainfall areas of Ikom in Cross River State, which is a strong candidate for a future regional_overrides entry once the specific numbers for each zone can be found. Yield figures were deliberately not touched this pass and still need their own sourcing effort.
version_history.source: MarNat StudySpace - Cocoa Production in Nigeria; Floratalk - How to Plant Cocoa in Nigeria; UKEssays - Cocoa Cultivation Practices in Nigeria; Veggie Grow - Cocoa Farming in Nigeria; FarmPays 2026 - Cocoa Farming In Nigeria; CRIN - Agronomy and Soils programme page; CRIN - Cocoa programme page; CRIN 2023 Annual Report; Status of cocoa swollen shoot virus disease in Nigeria (field survey); Black pod disease profile, Southwest Nigeria (biorxiv); Testing for resistance of CRIN hybrid cacao germplasm against Phytophthora megakarya (biorxiv)

version_history.changed_by: AgTrail Knowledge Base - platform bugfix, land-prep sequencing gate
version_history.summary: Bumped min_days_after_dependency from 0 to 1 on cocoa_r1, in response to a real bug the user found while using the platform: land preparation could be logged and the very next dependent stage logged on the SAME DAY, with no gap enforced at all, even though the workflow conceptually expects one stage to be completed/settled before the next begins. min=0 technically meant '0 or more days later', which permitted same-day submissions. This is a data-authoring fix (a deliberate rule-value choice), not an engine bug -- the engine was correctly enforcing exactly what the rule said, the rule just said something too permissive. No maximum-day-window or severity changed, and no other rule in this file was touched.
version_history.source: N/A -- internal platform bugfix, not new agronomic sourcing.

version_history.changed_by: AgTrail Knowledge Base - platform bugfix, second sequencing sweep
version_history.summary: Added cocoa_r_seq_fertilizer_application_weeding, cocoa_r_seq_weeding_pruning. Found via a systematic audit of every consecutive REQUIRED-to-REQUIRED workflow step pair across all 20 crops, run after the user asked whether the land-prep sequencing fix (first sweep) generalized to every stage transition. It did not -- this file had one or more later-stage transitions where the next required step could be logged with no record of the preceding required step ever existing, the same bug class as the original land-prep gap. min=1 day so same-day submissions are also caught. Confirmed via scenario testing that the affected operation(s) now correctly require their dependency to exist first.
version_history.source: N/A -- internal platform bugfix, not new agronomic sourcing.

The age limits themselves are unchanged.

yield_validation.source: AgTrail Master Agronomist & Validator Ruleset, Agrolinking Solutions Ltd., July 2026, section 15 (Cocoa). Yield is dry beans per hectare. The file had no yield limits before.

harvest_estimate.method: Typical is the FAO national average for Nigeria in 2024. The normal range is the standard range the crop's yield checks already use (the CEO's ruleset; for soybean, the IITA-based range). The harvest window is the expected window in the crop's timing rules. The range is what is normal for a farm, not a forecast for this one.
caveats: National averages hide the spread between farms, so a single farm can be well outside the typical figure.
FAO's national figures for Nigeria are compiled from national reports and FAO estimates and move little from year to year.
Not a prediction for this farm: it does not know this season's rain, soil, seed or care.
